Brand refresh · Social content system · 2026

Kept the recognition.
Removed the noise.

The Station Magazine covers music, fashion, culture and people in Lagos. It had a logo people already knew, but no typography and no system for showing up every day. I refined the mark, chose the type, and built a library of carousel templates the team now posts with daily.

The brief

A logo with no language around it.

The founder had a mark he liked: a serif T with a maroon S cutting through its stem. What he didn't have was anything around it. There were no brand fonts, no rules for posts, and every new graphic was started from scratch, so the magazine looked slightly different every day.

He also didn't know what typefaces suited the brand, so that became my job: research what an editorial culture magazine in Lagos should feel like, then make the logo, the type and the posts speak with one voice.

01 · The refresh

Drag to see what changed.

The original relied on gloss, bevels and highlights. I kept everything people recognised (the interlock, the serif, the black and maroon) and took the effects away, so the letterforms do the work.

Before After
  1. Removed

    Bevels, gloss and highlights

    Effects that dated the mark and turned muddy at small sizes or in print.

  2. Kept

    The T and S interlock

    The shape readers already knew, so the refresh felt like an upgrade, not a rebrand.

  3. Sharpened

    Flat black and maroon

    Two solid colours that print cleanly, embroider, and hold up on any background.

02 · The scale test

Where the refresh earns its keep.

A magazine logo lives as a profile photo, a watermark and a favicon far more often than on a cover. At those sizes, effects turn to noise.

03 · The system

A palette and type pairing pulled from the mark.

The type was chosen for one job each: a heavy condensed italic for headlines that need to stop a scroll, wide-tracked capitals for categories and navigation, and the serif monogram as the anchor that ties every post back to the brand.

Frame Red#6D0107
Monogram Maroon#913334
Ink#111111
Newsprint#E6DDD6

Anatomy of a cover post

  1. Frame Red border. Makes every post recognisable in a feed before anyone reads it.
  2. Monogram watermark. Sits behind the subject at low opacity, so the brand is present without competing.
  3. Condensed italic headline. Black with one line in maroon to carry the emphasis.
  4. Tracked category line. "Music / Fashion / Culture / People" tells new readers what the magazine covers.
  5. Swipe prompt. A quiet outlined button that pushes readers into the carousel.

04 · The templates

Built to be filled in, every single day.

The goal wasn't one beautiful post. It was a library the team could reuse, swapping photos and copy while the brand stays consistent. Each format has a fixed job.

05 · In motion

News posts that move.

For breaking music news, a motion template keeps the headline fixed while footage and oversized type play behind it. Readers get the story in the first second; the movement keeps them watching.

What I learned

The first direction didn't land, and that made the final one better.

My first identity direction used a typeface that looked good on its own but didn't match the magazine's personality. The client felt it straight away. Instead of polishing the same idea, I went back to research: what Lagos culture titles look like, what the existing mark was already saying, and which type would amplify it rather than fight it.

The lesson I carry into every brand project now: fonts aren't decoration, they're the brand's tone of voice. Get that right and everything else, from the logo to a daily carousel, falls into place.
